what: The Probability Calculator covers the four calculations students and analysts need most: combinations and permutations, the probability of two events, the binomial distribution, and the chance of something happening at least once in several tries.
Each answer comes with the formula used, so you can follow the working. Very large counts such as 1000C500 are calculated exactly.
It is useful for statistics classes, games and lotteries, quality control and everyday questions about chance. It runs in your browser.
uses: Count possible hands or tickets, such as 2,598,960 five-card poker hands from 52 cards.
Count arrangements with repetition, such as 10⁴ four-digit PINs.
Find the chance of A and B, A or B, neither or exactly one, for independent, dependent or mutually exclusive events.
Find the chance of exactly, at most or at least k successes in n trials.
Find the chance of at least one six in four dice rolls, or how many tries give a 50% chance.
tutorial: Pick Combinations and permutations, Two events, Binomial or At least once.

Enter the number of items n and how many are chosen r. You get nCr (order does not matter), nPr (order matters), both with repetition, and n!. Large values appear in scientific notation with the exact digits below.
Enter P(A) and P(B), and choose independent, dependent (then enter P(B given A)) or mutually exclusive. You get and, or, not, neither, exactly one and the conditional probabilities.

Enter the number of trials n, the success chance p and the number of successes k. You get P(X = k), at most, fewer than, at least and more than k, plus the mean and standard deviation, with a bar chart.
Enter the chance per try and the number of tries.
Decimals (0.25), percentages (25%) and fractions (1/4) all work.
features: Factorials, combinations and permutations use whole-number arithmetic with no rounding, up to n = 5,000.
Counting, two events, binomial and repeated trials.
Each result shows the formula and the numbers used.
Warns when probabilities contradict each other, such as P(A and B) larger than P(B).
See the whole distribution with your k highlighted, even for n = 100,000.

example.title: Worked example: 10 coin flips
example.text: On the Binomial tab, enter n = 10, p = 0.5 and k = 5. P(X = 5) = C(10, 5) × 0.5⁵ × 0.5⁵ = 252/1024 = 0.24609375, so exactly five heads happens about 24.6% of the time. P(X ≤ 5) = 0.623 and the mean is 5 with a standard deviation of 1.58.

tips: Use combinations when order does not matter (a hand of cards, a team) and permutations when it does (a race result, a PIN).
Independent means one event does not change the chance of the other, like two coin flips; drawing cards without putting them back is dependent.
Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen, so they are never independent unless one has probability 0.
For a binomial setting the trials must be independent and have the same chance of success each time.
problems: It says n must be a whole number
Counts of items and trials must be whole numbers of 0 or more.
Probabilities must fit together: P(A and B) cannot be bigger than P(A) or P(B), and P(A or B) cannot exceed 1.
r is larger than n: you cannot choose more different items than you have. With repetition it is possible, so that result is shown.
Use a number between 0 and 1, a percentage like 30%, or a fraction like 3/10.
